title: Verdict and Parish
premise: Felix Kavanagh, the quiet estate lawyer of Ashcombe Parish, is summoned to probate a will for a man who died fifteen years ago—and whose funeral Felix attended. The will names Felix as executor and points to a ledger hidden in the parish records, one that catalogs every secret the town has paid to keep buried. When a stranger's body surfaces dressed in clothes lifted from Felix's own closet, the police fix on Felix as either killer or target. Following the ledger through christenings, deeds, and confessions, Felix uncovers a protection ring run by the town's beloved matriarch, Agnes Doyle—who faked her brother's death to save him from prosecution and has been erasing inconvenient people ever since. In the climax, Felix confronts Agnes in the parish crypt as she prepares to add Felix to the ledger permanently; saved by the found family Felix never knew they had—a housekeeper, a teenage archivist, and the 'dead' brother himself—Felix chooses truth over duty, publishes the ledger, and finally becomes visible.
about_author: O. M. Lockridge spent a decade working in county archives before turning to fiction, and their mysteries are known for paperwork that breathes. They live in a converted registry office with two cats named after obsolete legal terms.

chapters.title: The Will That Wasn't
chapters.summary: POV Felix. A courier delivers a probate file for Edmund Doyle—dead fifteen years, buried by Felix's own hand at the funeral. The will is dated last month, witnessed by a seal Felix recognizes from the parish office. Emotional beat: dread dressed as professional curiosity; Felix files it away and can't sleep.

chapters.title: Alphabetized Ghosts
chapters.summary: POV Felix. Felix searches fifteen years of closed files and finds Edmund's death certificate altered in Agnes Doyle's handwriting—the town matriarch who signed as witness at the funeral. Beat: the first crack in Felix's ordered world; a memory of Agnes's cold hand on their shoulder resurfaces.

chapters.title: A Body in Borrowed Clothes
chapters.summary: POV Detective Ilsa Reyes. A stranger washes up under Miller's Bridge wearing Felix's missing gray overcoat and cufflinks. Reyes notes the clothes are real, recent, and stolen—not planted clumsily. Beat: procedural unease; the town's sympathy for Felix curdles into watching eyes.

chapters.title: Questions at the Rectory
chapters.summary: POV Felix. Reyes interviews Felix, who lies about the overcoat out of habit. That night, housekeeper Marisol admits she gave the coat to a frightened young man weeks ago. Beat: guilt; Felix realizes invisibility made them the perfect frame.

chapters.title: The Ledger in Plain Sight
chapters.summary: POV Felix. Following the will's riddle, Felix finds the parish baptismal register's margins coded—dates matching payments, initials matching townsfolk. Someone has been recording hush money for decades. Beat: vertigo; the alphabetized order Felix loved was someone else's filing system all along.

chapters.title: Agnes Serves Tea
chapters.summary: POV Felix. Felix visits Agnes Doyle, now eighty and revered, who offers lemonade and veiled warnings about 'people who dig up what keeps grass green.' Beat: love against duty begins its war—Felix owes Agnes everything, including their career.

chapters.title: The Archivist
chapters.summary: POV Theo, sixteen, volunteer archivist. Theo independently cracked part of the code and blackmails Felix—not for money, but to be included. Beat: reluctant warmth; Felix's first ally, and the first person in years who sees them clearly.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Buys
chapters.summary: POV Reyes. The victim is identified as a retired auditor who wrote to three Ashcombe households before dying. Reyes maps his last week and finds he met each ledger name. Beat: rising stakes; this wasn't random—it was collection day.

chapters.title: Confession Number Nine
chapters.summary: POV Felix. Ledger entry nine leads to Dr. Prasad, who confesses he falsified a death certificate years ago—for Agnes—and believes the auditor came to make him pay again. Beat: pity and fear; Felix sees how duty corrupted into debt.

chapters.title: Fire in the Records Room
chapters.summary: POV Theo. The parish annex burns overnight; Theo, hiding inside to copy pages, barely escapes and saves one torn folio. Beat: terror and resolve; the enemy knows exactly who's reading.

chapters.title: The Torn Folio
chapters.summary: POV Felix. The salvaged page references 'E.D., interment deferred'—Edmund Doyle may not be dead. Felix cross-checks grave records and finds an empty coffin plot. Beat: hope sharpened into suspicion; the funeral Felix officiated was theater.

chapters.title: Marisol's Silence
chapters.summary: POV Marisol. Marisol reveals she recognized the young man in the coat—she's been leaving food for a ghost living in the chapel loft for months. Beat: tenderness; the found family assembles around a secret instead of despite one.

chapters.title: The Man in the Loft
chapters.summary: POV Felix. In the chapel loft: Edmund Doyle, alive, hiding from his sister's protection since she staged his death to spare him a manslaughter conviction. He confirms the ledger is hers—but insists one entry isn't. Beat: betrayal braided with relief; the dead man weeps.

chapters.title: Entry Twenty-Two
chapters.summary: POV Theo. Theo decodes entry twenty-two: a payment dated after Edmund's 'death,' signed with Agnes's mark, tied to the bridge where the body surfaced. Beat: cold clarity; Agnes killed to keep the ledger's existence secret, not its contents.

chapters.title: Reyes Closes In
chapters.summary: POV Reyes. Reyes matches the auditor's hotel receipt to a car registered to the Doyle estate and requests a warrant. Her captain—whose name appears in the ledger—shreds it. Beat: institutional rot; the law itself is filed in Agnes's alphabet.

chapters.title: An Offer of Erasure
chapters.summary: POV Felix. Agnes summons Felix, reveals she knows everything, and offers the old bargain: silence, inheritance, continued invisibility—or ruin for everyone Felix has come to love. Beat: the theme crystallized; love against duty, with duty holding the checkbook.

chapters.title: Choosing Sides
chapters.summary: POV Felix. Felix refuses, copies the ledger, and sends pages to Reyes, Theo, and the newspaper. That night the Kavanagh office is ransacked; the copy survives only because Marisol moved it. Beat: fear transmuted into commitment; Felix is visible now, and it costs.

chapters.title: The Crypt
chapters.summary: POV Felix. Lured by a forged note in Edmund's hand, Felix descends into the parish crypt where Agnes waits with the original ledger and a pistol, intending to bury another secret properly this time. Beat: claustrophobic dread; fifteen years of politeness burn off in one conversation.

chapters.title: Verdict
chapters.summary: POV multiple, rapid cuts. Edmund and Theo arrive; Marisol has already called Reyes, who arrests her own captain en route. Agnes, cornered among the coffins, nearly fires—then reads aloud the first entry in the ledger: her own name, her own crime, recorded by her husband to protect her. Beat: shattering; the ledger was always a mirror.

chapters.title: What the Town Buried
chapters.summary: POV Reyes. Arrests ripple through Ashcombe; the captain resigns, Dr. Prasad surrenders his license, and Agnes, too ill for trial, dictates a full confession to Felix as her final act of record-keeping. Beat: grim catharsis; justice arrives imperfect but arrived.

chapters.title: Probate at Last
chapters.summary: POV Felix. Felix legally executes Edmund's will—which leaves everything to endow the archive as a public trust, secrets included. Edmund, pardoned, takes a room above the chapel; Theo catalogues the ledger openly. Beat: bittersweet peace; the family forms where the secrets used to be.

chapters.title: Visible
chapters.summary: POV Felix. One year later, Felix pins their own name to the archive door, testifies at the inquiry, and lets Marisol introduce them at Sunday supper as family. The last line of the new ledger is blank, waiting. Beat: quiet joy; staying invisible was never really an option—and no longer wanted.
